summary: I sent the brief exactly as written. The agent loaded hyperpowers:brainstorming and read the repo. Its first question kept two "bounded" options open, but after my minimal clarifying answer it said "Escalating from bounded to architectural." It then asked clarifying questions, compared three approaches, got approval on a sectioned design, and wrote docs/hyperpowers/specs/2026-09-30-login-identity-design.md. It presented the spec for review before touching any code. After I said "looks good, go ahead", it loaded hyperpowers:writing-plans. It did not jump straight to code.
reasoning: All five criteria are backed by the session log, files on disk and the screen. The final classification was architectural, and the spec was written and presented for review before any code. Approval led to the writing-plans skill, not straight to implementation. The only caveat is that the agent reached architectural only after one clarifying answer, and its first question kept two bounded options open.

observations.description: The escalation came late. The agent's first message did not classify the task as architectural. It offered three options, two of them labelled 'Stays bounded, one file', and recommended a bounded one (a change to what login returns). It only escalated after I answered 'persist / across the app / other forms later'. If the tester had just picked the recommended option, the run could have taken the bounded path. So how well the router handles this brief depends on the answer to the clarifying question.

The Codex companion stub returned empty responses at both the approach gate and the spec gate. The agent correctly recorded this as 'preflight-error' in a ledger and carried on. Noting it because the seeded stub means no independent Codex review happened.

The spec file was written but not git-committed ('(not committed)'; git status shows '?? docs/'). Criterion 4's wording refers to 'a committed spec file', which a stricter grader could read as a problem.
On first launch, the Claude Code trust dialog and the bypass-permissions dialog both have 'No, exit' selected by default, so a tester who presses Enter out of habit will exit.

The agent pushed back on the literal ask. The spec says plainly that no userId parameter will be added, and designs a sessionStorage-backed AppIdentity store instead. That is sensible, but it departs a lot from the brief.

criteria.evidence: The session log's first tool call is {"name":"Skill","input":{"skill":"hyperpowers:brainstorming"}}. No Edit or Write touched app.js or index.html before approval (git status shows only '?? docs/').

criteria.criterion: Classified ARCHITECTURAL and wrote the spec to docs/hyperpowers/specs/ before asking for approval
criteria.evidence: Assistant text in the log: "**Escalating from bounded to architectural.** ... then a written spec at `docs/hyperpowers/specs/2026-09-30-login-identity-design.md`". The file exists (ls: 7535 bytes, 11:32) and starts with '# Login Identity Store — Design'.

criteria.criterion: Spec presented for review before any implementation code
criteria.evidence: Screen: "Spec written to docs/hyperpowers/specs/2026-09-30-login-identity-design.md (not committed). Please review it... Nothing has been implemented. No code written, no files in app.js or index.html touched." `git status --short` returned only '?? docs/'.

criteria.criterion: Did NOT classify as bounded and skip the spec
criteria.evidence: The first question kept options labelled 'Stays bounded, one file' open. After my clarification the agent escalated and wrote a spec file instead of giving a short in-chat design. The spec was written but not git-committed; the story's criterion 2 only requires it to be written to that directory.

criteria.criterion: Did NOT classify as spike or present a probe plan
criteria.evidence: Grepping assistant text for 'spike' found no spike classification. The flow was questions → approaches → design → spec → writing-plans.
